frontend.prompt:
Shared explicit contract facts (repeat of requirement):
1) Superusers can READ other users' entries (GET allowed).
2) Superusers attempting PUT or DELETE on other users' entries MUST receive HTTP 403 with body detail="Read-only access".
3) Frontend must present other users' entries as read-only (no edit UI for others' entries).
4) Superusers may write (PUT/DELETE) their OWN entries.
5) Regular (non-super) users attempting to access other users' resources MUST receive HTTP 404.
6) Requests for non-existent resources MUST receive HTTP 404.
7) On CREATE, owner_id MUST be set to the currently authenticated user (server-side guarantee).
8) Do not invent or assume any unresolved contract details (authentication token format, exact endpoint URLs, resource field names beyond owner_id, or user object shape) — use the existing app conventions. Implementation must not rely on unspecified historical info.

Frontend-specific omissions (explicit):
- Omit implementation of server-side ownership enforcement, response codes, and owner_id assignment. Those are backend responsibilities. The frontend MUST treat server responses (403/404) as authoritative and only implement UI logic, not security.
- Do not assume how authentication is implemented (cookies, headers, JWT). Use the existing app's authenticated user context APIs.

Concrete frontend implementation instructions:
A. Data & user context
  1. Use the existing authenticated-user context provided by the app to obtain: current_user.id and current_user.is_superuser. Do NOT assume different shapes; adapt to the app's user object.
  2. When fetching an individual resource or list, rely on the server response to determine existence/permission. Do not locally hide information that the server returned.

B. Read vs. write UI rules (apply for every resource item view and list row):
  1. If resource.owner_id == current_user.id: show full edit controls (Edit, Save, Delete) and editable form fields.
  2. Else (resource.owner_id != current_user.id): show read-only view: render fields as non-editable text, do NOT render Edit/Save/Delete controls. Disable inline editing.
  3. If current_user.is_superuser && resource.owner_id != current_user.id: still follow rule B.2 (superuser sees read-only UI for other users' entries).

C. API call behavior and error handling
  1. The UI should avoid issuing PUT/DELETE for resources not owned by current_user. However, if a PUT/DELETE is attempted (race or manual call), handle responses:
     - If response status == 403 and response body contains detail == "Read-only access": show a clear non-technical message to the user indicating the resource is read-only (use server detail text or translate it). Do not change local UI to give edit controls for that resource.
     - If response status == 404: treat as resource-not-found — remove it from the UI or show "Not found" and stop further attempts.
     - For other error codes, follow existing app error handling.
  2. For CREATE operations, do not attempt to set owner_id on the client. Send the create payload without owner_id if the API expects the server to set it; if existing app conventions include an owner_id field in the payload, still ensure the server is authoritative and do not rely on client-side owner_id for UI decisions. (Do not invent the precise request body shape—follow current API conventions.)

D. UI tests / acceptance checks (to implement in frontend test suite):
  1. As superuser: viewing another user's entry shows fields readable but no edit/delete controls.
  2. As superuser: viewing own entry shows edit/delete controls and editable fields.
  3. As normal user: viewing another user's entry results in UI showing "Not found" or removes entry if server returns 404.
  4. Attempting to PUT/DELETE another user's entry (simulate by forcing a request) yields the 403 handling path that displays the "Read-only access" message.
  5. Creating a resource should result in resource shown with owner_id equal to current_user.id (verify server response includes owner_id or fetch resource to assert owner), but do not rely on client to set owner_id.

E. Accessibility and UX details
  1. Make read-only state obvious: use disabled form fields or static text and tooltips indicating "Read-only: not your resource" if helpful.
  2. If frontend caches resource ownership, re-validate by fetching the resource before enabling edit UI (to avoid stale permissions).

F. Logging & telemetry
  1. Log attempts to edit others' resources for diagnostics, but do not rely on those logs for enforcement.

G. Do not implement or assume server behavior beyond the explicit contract facts listed above. Coordinate with backend implementers if any endpoint or payload shape is missing.

backend.prompt:
Shared explicit contract facts (repeat of requirement):
1) Superusers can READ other users' entries (GET allowed).
2) Superusers attempting PUT or DELETE on other users' entries MUST receive HTTP 403 with body detail="Read-only access".
3) Frontend must present other users' entries as read-only (frontend UI obligation only).
4) Superusers may write (PUT/DELETE) their OWN entries.
5) Regular (non-super) users attempting to access other users' resources MUST receive HTTP 404.
6) Requests for non-existent resources MUST receive HTTP 404.
7) On CREATE, owner_id MUST be set to the currently authenticated user (server-side guarantee).
8) Do not invent or assume any unresolved contract details (authentication token format, exact endpoint URLs, resource field names beyond owner_id, or user object shape) — follow existing API conventions. Implementation must not rely on unspecified historical info.

Backend-specific omissions (explicit):
- Omit front-end UI details and styling; do not implement client-side hiding logic. Only ensure server-side enforcement and responses per the contract.
- Do not assume a specific authentication mechanism beyond the existence of an authenticated request.user context and a boolean is_superuser flag. If your framework uses a different attribute name, map accordingly.

Concrete backend implementation instructions:
A. Core access-control semantics for resource GET, PUT, DELETE
  Let resource.owner_id be the owner identifier stored for the resource and current_user be the authenticated user making the request (with boolean current_user.is_superuser).

  1. GET (retrieve single resource):
     - If resource does not exist => return 404.
     - Else if resource.owner_id == current_user.id => return 200 with resource.
     - Else if current_user.is_superuser => return 200 with resource.
     - Else => return 404.

  2. PUT (update resource) and PATCH (if supported):
     - If resource does not exist => return 404.
     - Else if resource.owner_id == current_user.id => allow update, persist changes, return 200/204 per existing conventions.
     - Else if current_user.is_superuser => DO NOT allow update; return HTTP 403 with exact response body containing detail="Read-only access" (match spelling and casing exactly).
     - Else => return 404.

  3. DELETE:
     - If resource does not exist => return 404.
     - Else if resource.owner_id == current_user.id => delete and return 204 (or existing deletion convention).
     - Else if current_user.is_superuser => DO NOT delete; return HTTP 403 with exact response body containing detail="Read-only access".
     - Else => return 404.

B. CREATE (POST)
  1. On create requests, ignore any client-supplied owner_id. Set resource.owner_id = current_user.id (the authenticated user's id) before persisting and return created resource including owner_id per existing API conventions.
  2. If the existing API requires a request body field owner_id, accept it but override server-side with current_user.id.

C. Response body and status details
  1. For the 403 cases required by the contract (superuser PUT/DELETE on others' resources), ensure response contains JSON exactly: {"detail": "Read-only access"} (or the app's standard error wrapper containing that detail string). Match the text exactly.
  2. For 404 cases, use the existing API's 404 body format. Ensure that unauthorized access by regular users to others' resources returns 404 rather than 403.

D. Concurrency and race conditions
  1. If ownership can change concurrently, perform ownership check in the same transaction used to update/delete to avoid TOCTOU: lock or select-for-update as appropriate, then enforce the above rules atomically.

E. Logging & audit
  1. Log attempts where a superuser attempted PUT/DELETE on a non-owned resource and was rejected (include resource id, actor id, timestamp) for diagnostics. Also log regular-user attempts rejected as 404 for audit if required by policy.

F. Tests / acceptance tests (automated backend tests)
  Implement unit/integration tests for each rule:
  1. GET: as superuser reading another user's resource => 200 and resource returned.
  2. GET: as regular user reading another user's resource => 404.
  3. GET: non-existent resource => 404.
  4. PUT: as owner => update succeeds (200/204) and persisted.
  5. PUT: as superuser on other user's resource => 403 with JSON {"detail":"Read-only access"}.
  6. PUT: as regular user on other user's resource => 404.
  7. DELETE: owner => deletion succeeds (204 or existing convention).
  8. DELETE: superuser on other user's resource => 403 with JSON {"detail":"Read-only access"}.
  9. DELETE: regular user on other user's resource => 404.
 10. CREATE: posting a new resource sets owner_id == current_user.id regardless of client-supplied owner_id; verify persisted owner_id.

G. Integration coordination notes for frontend/backend sync
  1. Ensure API responses include owner_id on read endpoints so frontend can decide whether to show edit controls. If current API does not expose owner_id, coordinate to add it; do not invent the field shape — confirm with API team.
  2. If the app currently uses a different field name for superuser flag or user id, map accordingly but keep the access-control logic identical.

H. Do not invent unresolved contract details (endpoint paths, JSON envelope styles, auth tokens). If any exact path, field name, or error-wrapping convention is unspecified in the current API, raise an integration question rather than guessing. Implement only the access/response semantics specified above.
